checkpoints: Reading the client IP from the first entry of `x-forwarded-for` without validating a trusted-proxy hop count treats an attacker-controlled header as ground truth: an attacker can send a different fabricated value on every request, so each request lands in a fresh rate-limit bucket and the counter never accumulates past 1 — a complete bypass rather than a partial weakening.

The correct fix for header-based client IP is configuring the trusted proxy chain to the actual hop count (for example `app.set('trust proxy', <hopCount>)`), so the framework strips client-injected entries and keeps only the value appended by the trusted load balancer.

Falling back to a per-process in-memory Map and returning true whenever the Redis-backed counter throws is a fail-open design for a security control: it turns a Redis outage into every replica running its own private, unshared counter, silently multiplying the effective rate limit by replica count and going dark exactly when it's needed most.

An abuse control like a login rate limiter must fail closed on a counter-store error — rejecting the request during an outage costs some availability, but a control that silently opens exactly when a distributed brute-force attack is most likely to be running is worse than no control at all.

Setting `user.locked = true` permanently once failed-login count reaches a threshold, with no code path anywhere to clear it, converts the lockout mechanism into a weapon: anyone who knows a victim's email can lock that account on purpose with five wrong passwords, forcing a support ticket to recover.

A safer response to repeated failed logins is exponential backoff per account combined with a CAPTCHA challenge after repeated failures, since this keeps raising the attacker's cost without ever handing an anonymous requester a permanent-lockout button against someone else's account.

Verifying a fix like this needs adversarial tests, not a single manual check from one tester: a request series rotating a forged `x-forwarded-for` value on every call must still return 429 by the expected attempt, a chaos test with the counter store stopped must show the request rejected rather than admitted, and repeated wrong-password attempts must show growing delay or a CAPTCHA challenge rather than a permanent lock.

Prioritizing PR findings by exploitability rather than by code style separates two complete bypasses — the spoofable rate-limit key and the fail-open counter fallback — from a design flaw with user-facing harm — the permanent lockout — with attacker impact, not stylistic preference, deciding what blocks approval.

Commenting out the per-test cleanup hook while both flows share one test file turns Flow 2 into a hidden dependent of Flow 1: it asserts against the exact row Flow 1 just committed, so filtering to run Flow 2 alone, reordering the tests, or running them in parallel all break it immediately.
When an earlier flow in the same suite fails partway through, every flow that runs after it cascades into a false red even though nothing is actually wrong with that later flow's own logic.

A missing connection-pool teardown is a separate defect from the missing per-test cleanup, not a side effect of it — a suite can have full order independence restored and still leave the app/DataSource open at the end.

`app.close()` is what triggers `onModuleDestroy` and releases resources like the TypeORM connection pool; without it the Postgres socket stays open and the test runner cannot exit the process on its own.

Locally an unclosed handle shows up as a Ctrl+C annoyance, but in CI there is no one to kill the process, so the job runner waits for a natural exit and hangs until it burns its own timeout budget — real pipeline time lost on every run.

`expect(res.body).toEqual({...})` performs a strict deep comparison over the entire response body, so any field the server adds later breaks every test using it even when the core behavior under test is still correct.

Copying the actual received value of a nondeterministic field like `createdAt` into the expected object just to make a `toEqual` assertion pass is a sign the assertion is checking the wrong thing — a shape check such as `expect.any(String)` alongside a narrower `toMatchObject` on the fields that matter targets the real behavior instead.

Preserving the original speed win doesn't require deleting the cleanup outright — narrowing the truncate to only the table or rows the suite actually touches keeps most of the time savings while restoring test independence.

In an e2e suite, wall-clock time decomposes into N × boot cost + N × cleanup cost + N × actual request work; when the requests themselves take milliseconds, the fixture lifecycle (app boot, cleanup, re-seed) — not the tests' own logic — is what dominates the runtime.

A full app boot (compiling the Nest DI container and opening the TypeORM connection) produces a running app that is identical for every test in the file, so building it fresh inside `beforeEach` pays that cost N times for no benefit; moving it to `beforeAll` (or an equivalent once-per-file/shared-fixture scope) collapses N× boot cost to 1×, since what a test needs is a running app, not a newly compiled one.

A per-test `TRUNCATE ... CASCADE` that wipes every table — including reference/master data the tests never mutate — forces that reference data to be re-seeded before every single test even though it never changes; narrowing the truncate to only the tables the tests actually write to removes this redundant re-seed cost.

`RESTART IDENTITY` on a truncate keeps auto-increment IDs from leaking across tests even when the truncate scope is narrowed to just the mutated tables, so shrinking cleanup scope does not require giving up ID predictability between tests.

Reference/master data can be seeded once in `beforeAll` right after the app boots, with the single full-table wipe (including that reference data) deferred to `afterAll` right before the app closes — this replaces N re-seeds with one.

Narrowing what gets rebuilt or truncated per test does not change the isolation guarantee: every test still starts from an empty state for the tables it touches — only the mechanism producing that state gets cheaper, not what is promised to the test author.

Skipping the truncate of tables that tests actually mutate in order to save time is a different kind of change from narrowing cleanup scope: it lets mutated rows leak between tests and trades correctness for speed, which is why it must be rejected even under time pressure.

A speed-up claim needs two kinds of proof: running the suite with shuffled order or single-test (`.only`) isolation confirms no test silently depends on state left behind by another, and a recorded before/after wall-clock measurement confirms the suite actually got faster rather than the improvement being assumed.

A UI e2e suite that repeats a full browser login before every test pays that ~3s cost once per test for zero new information, since login success is already proven after the first test — the resulting suite slowdown scales with the number of tests, not with the number of distinct things being verified.

Recording a trace, video, and screenshot on every run regardless of outcome is a separate, unrelated cost from the login overhead: this data exists to aid debugging, but a passing test is never debugged, so paying the recording cost on passing runs buys nothing.

Playwright's `storageState` mechanism amortizes login across a suite: a `globalSetup` script performs the one real login the suite needs in its own browser context and serializes cookies and localStorage to a file; every other test's context then loads that file via `use.storageState`, starting already authenticated in a few hundred milliseconds instead of repeating the ~3s login flow.

The storage state file must be written only after the post-login redirect is confirmed (e.g., after `page.waitForURL` resolves), not the instant the login click resolves — saving state before the redirect lands bakes a half-authenticated or still-on-login-page session into the file, and every test that loads it then fails for a reason unrelated to what it actually tests.

The spec that verifies the login flow itself must still open a fresh browser context with no `storageState` loaded; reusing the shared authenticated state there would mean the login form is never actually exercised again, silently losing coverage on the exact mechanism the rest of the suite now depends on.

Amortizing login into one stored session introduces a new failure mode: the token baked into the storage state carries its own TTL, and if that TTL is shorter than the total suite runtime, tests running late fail with unrelated 401s that look like flakiness — mitigated by using long-lived tokens in the test environment or re-minting the storage state partway through a long run.

Playwright's `trace`, `video`, and `screenshot` options can be scoped to failure conditions instead of left always-on: `trace: 'on-first-retry'` and `screenshot: 'only-on-failure'` still capture everything needed to diagnose a failing test while adding zero recording cost to tests that pass.

The login-overhead fix and the diagnostics-overhead fix are independent because they have different root causes — redundant repeated work versus unconditional instrumentation — and different solutions — state caching versus conditional recording — so treating them as one problem risks fixing only half the slowdown.

A test that passes in isolation but fails when run alongside others—especially when the failing test changes depending on execution order—signals shared mutable state between tests, not an incorrect assertion count.

Building `mockRepo` with `vi.fn()` at `describe`-scope creates it only ONCE, because Vitest runs the `describe` body a single time per file; that same object, along with its recorded-calls array and any `mockResolvedValue` stub, is reused unmodified by every `it` block inside it.

The `beforeEach` hook here only rebuilds the Nest testing module and re-fetches `service` from it — it never touches `mockRepo`, so nothing resets the mock's call history or stubbed return values between tests.

Because a `vi.fn()`'s call history persists until explicitly cleared, `toHaveBeenCalledOnce()` in one test and `not.toHaveBeenCalled()` in another read from the same accumulating counter rather than a fresh one per test.

Execution order only decides which assertion trips first, not whether the bug exists: swapping the two `it` blocks moves the failure to the other test, since whichever runs second inherits the stale call count left behind by the one that ran first.

This is a violation of the Isolated principle from F.I.R.S.T.: every test must start from a known, clean state, and no test's outcome should depend on which other tests ran before it or in what order.

The one-line fix is calling `vi.clearAllMocks()` as the first statement inside `beforeEach`, before the testing module is rebuilt — it resets every mock's call history and configured return values so each test starts from a clean slate.

Rerunning the file with the tests in their original order, then swapped or shuffled, and seeing green in every ordering confirms the fix; the same file is worth sweeping afterward for other leaks of this class, such as a `vi.useFakeTimers()` call left active without a matching `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach`.
